Eval 1 (without skill) — copy/paste feedback
drift_report.txt
Verdict: Strong report, but not tool-faithful to the OKF skill

This is a high-signal drift report. It goes beyond naive path matching and correctly notices that the latest three commits are OKF/doc migration churn, then widens the analysis window to the real memory/chat-persistence code changes. The tiered worklist is useful: Tier A gives concrete stale reference docs, explains why each is likely stale, and names the missing capabilities to document.

What’s strong

Good window choice: skips misleading recent docs-only commits and analyzes the real code-change line.
Good prioritization: Tier A/B/C/D makes the worklist actionable instead of dumping raw grep hits.
Strong stale-doc evidence: checks old reference docs for absence of new concepts like MemoryRecalled, MEMORY_SUPPRESSED, ThreadStore, suppress routes, and thread CRUD.
Correct report-only behavior: no docs edited.
Better than the simpler script output for broad “are docs stale?” detection, because it catches stale architecture/reference docs that may not mention exact changed paths.
Main caveat

This does not appear to use the skill’s canonical drift_report.py; it uses custom /tmp/drift_scan*.py symbol extraction. That makes the report stronger, but less reproducible against the eval’s expected Routine 3/tooling path. If the eval is meant to test the OKF curator workflow, mark this as “excellent analysis, but non-standard implementation.”
Potential issues to fix

The prompt asks for “which docs reference code that just changed.” Some Tier A findings are symbol/concept correlated rather than explicit file-path references. That is fine, but the report should state: “These docs matched changed-code symbols, not necessarily literal file paths.”
Tier A should include the exact changed source files per doc, not only prose. Example: AGENT_UI_ADAPTER_ARCHITECTURE.md ↔ agent_ui_adapter/wire/domain_events.py, agent_ui_adapter/server.py.
“No doc files were read into / written by this analysis beyond grepping” is awkward: grepping is reading. Say “No docs were modified; docs were only scanned.”
If this is judged against the skill routine, add a note explaining why the canonical drift_report.py was insufficient and why custom symbol matching was used.
Recommended edits before accepting

Add a short “match type” field per Tier A item: literal path, symbol, or concept absence.
Add the changed source file(s) driving each Tier A/B recommendation.
Add a reproducibility command or attach the temporary scan script logic, since /tmp/drift_scan.py is not preserved.
Add one sentence that this is a broader semantic drift scan, not just the baseline path-reference drift report.
transcript.md
Verdict: Accept

Good audit trail. It explains the window choice, the custom scan method, the last-substantive-edit correction, and confirms no docs were edited.

Nit: Since the analysis depends on temporary /tmp scripts, the transcript should either include their rough algorithm or say they were not preserved. Otherwise the report is hard to reproduce exactly.

grading.json
Verdict: Pass, but grader is too shallow

The three assertions pass:

drift report produced
report-only, no docs edited
report names changed code + docs
But the grader does not distinguish:

canonical drift_report.py workflow vs custom semantic scan
literal code-path references vs symbol/concept matches
raw worklist vs judged stale-doc verdict
Add an assertion like: “report explains drift window and matching method,” and optionally: “each worklist item maps to a changed source file or symbol.”

Overall eval verdict
Accept as a stronger human-quality drift report. It answers the user’s real question well and gives a better worklist than the basic path-matching script.

Caveat for skill eval: It is less faithful to the OKF curator Routine 3 tooling because it appears to use custom symbol extraction rather than the bundled drift_report.py. If the eval is testing skill adherence, score it slightly below the with-skill run on reproducibility, but above it on depth of stale-doc discovery.
